author: Sophocles
title: The laws and the city
where: *Antigone*: the elders’ song on man, Antigone’s answer, Creon and his son
about: Two brothers have killed each other fighting over Thebes, and Creon, the new king, orders that one lie unburied on pain of death; their sister Antigone buries him. The first passage ends a song that the chorus, the city’s elders, sing before they know who did it. In the second Antigone, caught, answers the king (two and a half lines are left out at the dots), and in the third Creon quarrels with his son Haemon, who is to marry her. The English is F. Storr’s verse translation of 1912.

view.says: In 1941 Auden made Antigone his instance of the hero who accepts a tragic choice: seeing that she cannot both obey the law and do her duty to her brother, she chooses, and her death is her own will. In 1967 he held that for Sophocles the chief figure is Creon: Antigone’s part is to reveal his hubris, the overconfidence of a man who thinks himself a god, beyond suffering.
view.quote: because she realizes that she cannot do both, she is free to choose, chooses, and wills her death
view.source: “James Joyce and Richard Wagner,” *Common Sense*, March 1941, in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 116; “The Martyr as Dramatic Hero,” in *Secondary Worlds* (1968), p. 19; on what hubris is, “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 19

plates.heading: The elders end their song on man

lenses.label: Greek
lenses.caption: The elders name two things for a man to honor: the laws of the land, and what Storr calls the Gods of the State, which in the Greek is the gods’ justice, sworn by oath. The man who honors both is hypsipolis, one word made of high and city. Next to it stands its opposite, apolis, cityless: the man whose daring brings him to wrong. The stanza asks for law and justice together. In the second passage Antigone says that Justice made no such laws as Creon’s. Auden’s Antigone owes one duty to her dead brother and one to her city, and must break one.
lenses.why: The elders ask for the land’s laws and the gods’ sworn justice together, a high city for the man who keeps both and none for the man who dares wrong; Auden’s Antigone must fail her brother or her city.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Greek of lines 365 to 375, with Liddell and Scott under *hypsipolis*, *apolis*, *enorkos*, *tolma* and *parestios*, and Jebb’s notes on lines 369 to 372. The gods’ justice follows the translation at Perseus; Jebb himself reads justice sworn by the gods. Antigone’s words about Justice are in [her answer to Creon](#/read/antigone/p3:36). Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 19.

notes.note: Sophocles has the two the other way round: his man goes at one time to evil, at another to good.
In the second passage Creon asks Antigone whether she dared overstep these *nomoi*, the same noun.

Word for word: of the gods, oath-bound, justice. The editor Jebb takes it as the justice a man has sworn by the gods to uphold; the Perseus revision of his translation takes it as the gods’ justice, to which he is bound by oath.
A compound of *high* and *city*: the dictionary gives citizen of a proud city, and Jebb’s note takes it as having a high city, not standing high in his city.
The dictionary’s first sense is without city or country; for this line it gives another, no true citizen, the opposite of *hypsipolis*, which stands next to it.
The dictionary gives courage and, in a bad sense, over-boldness; Creon uses the verb made from it in the second passage, where Storr again says *bold*.
Sophocles has *parestios*, by or at the hearth: may the man who does these things never be at my hearth.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.caption: Each line has six beats, with one or two syllables between them, and four of the six have a pause after the third. A handbook of verse says that lines of more than five beats tend to break up into smaller units. The speeches as a rule go in five beats without rhyme; the song leaves that line, as Sophocles here leaves spoken verse for song. The beat is Storr’s: Auden notes that unrhymed Greek verse, measured by syllable length, and rhymed English verse share nothing but rhythm. Twice Storr sets half against half: the light against counsels of ill, a standing city against a man with none.
lenses.why: Where Sophocles passes from speech to song, Storr passes from the five-beat line of the speeches to a six-beat line in two halves, and twice the halves carry the stanza’s alternatives: light or ill, a standing city or none.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, placed by ear. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapters 3 and 4, on lines of more than five beats, blank verse and Greek verse measured by length. Aristotle’s *Poetics*, chapters 4, 6 and 12, on speech and song; [the guard’s speech before the song](#/read/antigone/p2:64) for the five-beat line. Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 5.
lenses.meterName: six beats to the line, mostly three and three, with one or two syllables between the beats

points.say: Here the phrase runs on past the third beat, and the line has no pause inside it.
*Now* stands once in each half of the line. Said as a contrast, it takes the beat both times; *man*, just before the first, can also be heard stressed.
*City* takes a beat in each half: the city that stands, then *cityless*.

The dictionary stresses this word on its first syllable, and so it takes the line’s first beat. Said lightly, as a run-up to the next word, it leaves the line five beats, and the inner rhyme then falls on the second.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The rhyme is Storr’s. Greek verse as a rule had none. The line ends rhyme in pairs: skill with ill, State with rate, depart with heart. The lines rhyme midway too: flight with light, land with stand, pride with side. Each pair of long lines is also four short ones rhymed by turns. In Sophocles man’s skill brings him now to evil, now to good. Storr has the other order, and ill comes last, where it rhymes with skill. Storr held that a translation must be English before anything else. Auden thought it almost a rule that the more a version succeeds as English verse, the less it resembles the Greek.
lenses.why: Storr adds rhyme, twice a line, to a song with none in the Greek, and where skill rhymes with ill Sophocles’ order is reversed; Auden almost makes it a rule that success as English verse costs likeness to the Greek.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Baum, chapter 5 (Greek verse rejected rhyme) and chapter 4 (a short quatrain printed as a long couplet). The Greek of line 367 and Jebb’s translation of it, for the order of evil and good. Storr’s introduction to his *Sophocles* (1912), p. xii; Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 5.

lenses.label: Song
lenses.caption: This stanza is the last of four. The song follows a guard’s report that someone has buried the body; the elders do not know who. Three stanzas count what man has mastered: sea and earth; bird, beast and fish; speech, thought, city life, shelter. For death alone he has found no cure. The fourth turns from his power to its use. In the Greek the last two stanzas each set two opposites side by side: all-inventive and resourceless, high-citied and cityless. Auden wrote that the tragic hero is a warning to the chorus, and the man to imitate is the moderate citizen who keeps the law.
lenses.why: Three stanzas count man’s power and the fourth judges its use and praises the keeper of the laws; Auden says the tragic hero is a warning to the chorus, and the man to imitate is the moderate, law-keeping citizen.
lenses.stands: The song as printed here, from [its first stanza](#/read/antigone/p2:67) to the elders’ sight of Antigone, and [the guard’s report](#/read/antigone/p2:33) before it. The Greek of lines 360 to 362 and 370, with Liddell and Scott under *pantoporos*, *aporos* and *hypsipolis*. Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 19–20.
lenses.what: the song on man: its four stanzas, what comes before it and what comes after

facts.tells: a guard reports that someone has strewn dust on the body, done the rites and gone without a trace; Creon swears to punish the guards with worse than death unless they find the man, and goes in
wonders are many and none is a greater wonder than man: he crosses the stormy sea, and year after year his plows work the Earth, oldest of the gods
he snares birds, wild beasts and the fish of the sea; he tames the bull and the mountain deer, and breaks the horse to the bit

he has taught himself speech, quick thought and the ways of a city, and how to shelter from rain and frost; he is ready for everything and has learned to bear disease; against death he has found no remedy

his skill, past all thinking, leads him now to good, now to ill; if he honors the land’s laws and the gods his city stands proud; the man who boldly leaves the right path has no city, and the elders will not sit beside him or think as he does
the elders see Antigone led in and ask whether she has defied the king’s order

lenses.label: Sides
lenses.caption: Creon asks whether she dared break the law. Her answer makes the one law two, and the marks sort its terms. On the king’s side: these human laws, a mortal man, a breath. On the gods’ side: Zeus, Justice, and the unwritten laws of Heaven, which she describes by what they are not: unwritten, unchanging, not born today nor yesterday, undying. Sophocles sets the same contraries close together, and the name for that is antithesis. As Auden saw her in 1941, Antigone has to choose between the law and her duty to her brother. The ambiguity, he wrote, belongs to her situation and not to her: she refuses to leave it ambiguous.
lenses.why: Asked about the law, she splits it in two and sets the terms of a mortal king against the terms of the gods; for Auden in 1941 the ambiguity is in her situation, and she refuses to leave it ambiguous.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Greek of lines 450 to 457, which sets the same things against each other. Antithesis as the Online Etymology Dictionary and *Silva Rhetoricae* give it. Auden, “James Joyce and Richard Wagner” (1941), in *Prose*, vol. II, p. 116.
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build; here what is the king’s against what is the gods’

lenses.label: Knowing
lenses.caption: Creon has asked whether she knew of his order. Storr gives her the verb three times in one line: knew, knew, know. A word brought back in a changed form is called polyptoton. Sophocles has the verb once in that line and twice below, where the marks stand: no one knoweth where the gods’ laws came from, and I know that I must die. To die sooner she counts as gain. In Auden’s account of 1941 her freedom comes from seeing that she cannot both obey the law and do her duty to her brother: she chooses, and the death that follows is one she wills.
lenses.why: Know comes back through her answer: she knew the order, and she knows she must die and counts it gain; Auden’s Antigone of 1941 sees that she cannot do both, makes her choice and wills the death it brings.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and [Creon’s question](#/read/antigone/p3:30) just before it. Polyptoton as Merriam-Webster and *Silva Rhetoricae* define it. The Greek of lines 448, 457 and 460, with Liddell and Scott under *exoida*. Auden, “James Joyce and Richard Wagner” (1941), in *Prose*, vol. II, p. 116.
lenses.name: polyptoton
lenses.plain: one root repeated in different forms; here *knew* and *know* in one line, and the verb returns twice below

lenses.label: Greek
lenses.caption: In Sophocles’ Greek Creon asks if she dared overstep the laws. Two lines earlier, before the passage begins, he called his order a thing proclaimed. She takes up that word, the herald’s, three times here: Zeus did not have this cried; your proclamations, Storr’s a breath, have no such strength; she must die even had he not proclaimed it. Laws she says once, in a line the editors correct: Justice set no such laws among men. She denies that a mortal’s proclamations can override the gods’ usages, unwritten and not liable to fall. For Auden the decree, though perhaps too vindictive, is not plainly evil; Creon’s guilt is hubris toward the gods.
lenses.why: In the Greek Creon calls his order laws; three times she calls it a thing proclaimed, which cannot override the gods’ unwritten usages; for Auden the decree is not plainly evil, and Creon’s guilt is hubris toward the gods.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Greek of lines 447 to 461, with Liddell and Scott under *hyperbaino*, *kerysso*, *kerygma*, *prokerysso*, *hypertrecho*, *agraptos*, *asphales* and *nomimos*, and Jebb’s note and translation at lines 450 to 452. Auden, *Secondary Worlds* (1968), pp. 18–19.

notes.note: Creon’s verb is made from *tolma*, the daring of the elders’ song.
Creon’s noun is *nomoi*, laws, and his verb means to step over, and so to transgress.
Sophocles has only a pronoun, these things; the word *laws* in this line is Storr’s.
Here her word is *nomoi*, laws, as Storr’s Greek text and Jebb’s print the line (Justice set no such laws among men); the manuscripts have the gods setting these laws, the laws of burial.
Sophocles has *kerygmata*, things cried by a herald, where Storr has *a breath*; it is the play’s first word for the order, at line 8.
Creon’s verb means to step over; hers means to run over or beyond, to outrun, and in this line, the dictionary says, to prevail against.
Sophocles has two adjectives, unwritten and not liable to fall, and the noun *nomima*, usages or customs, which the dictionary says is almost the same as laws here.
The same verb with a prefix: to proclaim by herald, publicly.

plates.heading: Creon and Haemon, a line each

lenses.label: Exchange
lenses.caption: After a long speech each, father and son trade single lines, twenty-eight in all; ten are shown. This is stichomythia. In it, the dictionary says, one speaker usually opposes or corrects the other, often by repeating part of his words. The colors mark words taken up: the city (commons, mob, State), ruling, and woman. Sophocles has all three. Auden held that Antigone’s part in the play is to reveal Creon’s hubris toward the gods. The first line here asks about her. By the seventh Creon claims the State is his who rules it. Four lines past the last shown, Haemon tells him that he spurns the gods’ due.
lenses.why: In single lines each takes up the other’s words, and within seven lines a question about Antigone becomes Creon’s claim that the city is its ruler’s; Auden says her part in the play is to reveal his hubris.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a count of the lines of [the scene](#/read/antigone/p4:0) as printed here. Stichomythia as Liddell and Scott give it, and as the *Century Dictionary* describes it in the Online Etymology Dictionary. The Greek of lines 730 to 757; [Haemon’s line about the gods](#/read/antigone/p4:50). Auden, *Secondary Worlds* (1968), p. 19.
lenses.name: stichomythia
lenses.plain: two speakers answer each other a line at a time, often taking up each other’s words

lenses.label: City
lenses.caption: Where Storr has commons, mob and State, Sophocles gives both men one word, polis, or a word built on it: a city, and the body of its citizens. Mob, slang of the 1680s for the rabble, is Storr’s: Creon says the city. Monarch is close: Sophocles has rule alone, the two Greek words behind the English one. Desert is an empty land. The elders sing that the man who honors the laws has a high city, and Creon’s first speech has the same noun for laws: by such laws, or rules, he strengthens the city. His son tells him that a city owned by one man is no city.
lenses.why: Storr’s commons, mob and State go back to one Greek word, polis; Creon said his rules strengthen the city, the elders that the law-keeper’s city stands high, and now Haemon tells him that one man’s city is no city.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Greek of lines 733 to 739 and of line 191, with Liddell and Scott under *polis*, *homopolis*, *eremos* and *auxano*, and Jebb’s translation of lines 191 and 739. The Online Etymology Dictionary under *mob*, *monarch* and *monarchy*. [Creon’s first speech](#/read/antigone/p2:2) and [the end of the elders’ song](#/read/antigone/p2:73) as printed here.

notes.note: Sophocles has *homoptolis leos*, the people of the same city; Jebb’s note gives the united folk of Thebes.
Creon says the city; *mob* is English slang of the 1680s for the rabble, shortened from *mobile*.
The dictionary gives city, and also the community or body of citizens; Sophocles has the word once in this line, where Storr has *State* twice.
Creon asks whether the city is not held to be its ruler’s; Storr makes it a statement.
Sophocles has *archois monos*, you would rule alone; *monarch* comes from Greek *monos*, alone, and *arkhein*, to rule.
The dictionary gives desolate, lonely, solitary and, of places, empty. Jebb has *a desert* too.

lenses.label: Play
lenses.caption: In Storr’s English Creon speaks 339 of the play’s 1,279 lines and Antigone 205. After her last line, 883, come 396 more: the prophet Teiresias warns Creon, he gives way too late, and news comes of her death, his son’s and his wife’s. The messenger says Creon was a man to envy and now all is gone. That is the course Auden gives the hero of Greek tragedy in general: honored and fortunate when the play begins, in exceptional suffering when it ends. In 1967 he said that for Sophocles the play’s chief figure is Creon. Of the single speakers Creon has the most lines, and the last words before the elders end the play.
lenses.why: Sophocles gives Creon about two-thirds more lines than Antigone and keeps the play going for about four hundred lines after her last, down to his ruin, which agrees with Auden’s later view that for Sophocles the chief figure is Creon.
lenses.stands: A count of each speaker’s lines in the text printed here, a line being one printed line (five lines split between two speakers count for each), and in the Greek by its usual line numbers. What follows Antigone’s exit is in [the last part of the play](#/read/antigone/p5:0), with [the Messenger’s first speech](#/read/antigone/p5:91) and [Creon’s last lines](#/read/antigone/p5:176). Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 19; *Secondary Worlds* (1968), p. 19.
lenses.what: who speaks in the play and for how many lines, and where Antigone leaves it

facts.speaker: all speakers, after Antigone’s last line

auden.says: In a lecture of 1967 Auden takes Antigone as a martyr from before Christianity. Since every society abhors a traitor, he says, Creon’s decree may be thought too vindictive, but it is not plainly evil. What ruins Creon is punishment for his hubris toward the gods and not for how he treats Antigone, which is a sign of that hubris. If she had obeyed, some other course of events would in time have brought it out and brought a like punishment on him.
auden.quote: For Sophocles, the principal figure in the tragedy is not Antigone, but Creon.
auden.source: “The Martyr as Dramatic Hero,” in *Secondary Worlds* (the T. S. Eliot Memorial Lectures of 1967; 1968), pp. 18–19

auden.says: In 1948 Auden wrote that the tragic hero of the Greeks is a warning, and that the warning is meant for the chorus, who are ordinary citizens. The hero begins the play honored and fortunate and ends it suffering more than they do, because he has run against a law of right that binds everyone. Usually he could not have avoided it: every course open to him is wrong, and Antigone is one of four examples. Such a position is the sign of another guilt, hubris. Watching him fall, the chorus learns that strength tempts its owner to impiety, and that what makes the gods gods is their justice.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us” (the introduction to *The Portable Greek Reader*, 1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 19

auden.says: He goes on to say what each citizen of the democracy ought to aim at being: a moderate man who keeps the law and has no wish to outdo everyone else in strength or fame, and not the Homeric hero.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 19–20

auden.says: On reading the Greeks in English, Auden held that Greek literature in translation can no longer be approached as an aesthetic matter, since so much is lost between Greek and English that the loss is all but fatal. Among the obstacles he lists: Greek verse is unrhymed and measured by syllable length; Greek shows by the forms of its words what English shows by their order; Greek has compound epithets in plenty and English has few. Of dialogue in single lines he says that a version in plain modern idiom loses something essential to the Greek manner, which decks plain question and answer out as riddles.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 5–7

caveats: Auden’s reading list sets the *Antigone*, as an alternative to the *Agamemnon*, in the translation of Dudley Fitts and Robert Fitzgerald (1939); the English here is F. Storr’s of 1912, and the beat, the rhyme and the choice of English words are Storr’s.

Auden’s sentences of 1941 and 1967 about the play were read here only in snippets of scanned copies and not in full; the page of the 1941 sentences was worked out from the page headings near them, not seen.

The counts of lines are of Storr’s English as printed here, where five lines split between two speakers count for each; in the Greek, by the usual line numbers, Creon has 358 lines of 1,353 and Antigone 215, and the chorus, with 362, has four more than Creon.

The beats were marked by ear: *man* in the second line shown and the end of *outcast* in the fourth can be heard with more stress, and the fifth has six beats only if *Whoso* is stressed on its first syllable, as the dictionary gives it.

Two of the Greek readings followed here are editors’ corrections of the manuscripts, the verb for *honors* in the song (line 368) and *such laws* in Antigone’s answer (line 452); and in line 369 *the gods’ justice* can also be read, with Jebb, as justice sworn by the gods.
